overview: The Crete shown here around 300 to 200 BCE was an island of rival Greek city-states, including Knossos, Gortyn and Lyttos. Its single map colour hides shifting alliances and separate governments. This card concerns Hellenistic Crete, long after the Bronze Age palaces; the outline does not represent one unified Cretan kingdom.

periods.title: Hellenistic cities and alliances
periods.summary: Independent cities competed, negotiated and drew outside powers into their conflicts.

items.text: A decree from Itanos records a decision of its council and assembly to honour Patroklos, a Macedonian commander sent by King Ptolemy. They granted him citizenship and honours that also extended to his descendants. A powerful foreign friend could become part of a city’s political family.

Itanos guarded sea routes as well as land. Archaeologists date one southwestern fortification tower between the middle fourth and middle third centuries BCE. They suggest, cautiously, that Ptolemaic troops may have built it. Its strong masonry is firmer evidence than the proposed identity of its builders.

War could reach people who never carried a shield. In his account of the conflict around 220 BCE, Polybius says Knossian forces burned Lyttos while its army was away and carried its women and children to Knossos. Returning soldiers found refuge with their allies at Lappa.

At Lato, the main street climbed from a fortified gate toward the agora, the central public space. Excavators identified shops and workshops on one side and homes on seven terraces on the other. Much of the visible town belongs to the fourth and third centuries BCE.

A large underground reservoir near the centre of Lato is interpreted as the public cistern because of its size and position. Carrying and storing water mattered in a hill town. A useful public building could be mostly hidden beneath everyone’s feet.

Lato’s prytaneion, a civic building, contained a hall with a central hearth and space reconstructed for about eight dining couches. The city’s magistrates, called kosmoi, ate there and received official guests. Hospitality could be part of government business, with dinner built into the architecture.

The great stairway at Lato also served as a gathering place. Its straight rows of steps could seat an estimated eighty people watching ceremonies or public events in the agora. Narrower stairs divided the seating into sections, so getting to your place need not mean climbing over every neighbour.

House A at Nissi-Eleutherna began in the third century BCE and was used again in a later phase. Its plan includes a courtyard, sleeping spaces, a kitchen, storage and a work-and-living room with a cistern. The varied spaces show how several household needs fitted together within one building.

Later, in the late second or early first century BCE, that house also became a pottery workshop. Lead clamps and a repaired vessel reveal that people mended crockery as well as making it. Grinding equipment, loomweights and stored cereals belong to its domestic story too. These finds are later than this map’s displayed century.

Comparing houses at Lato and Trypetos, archaeologist Ruth Westgate found arrangements unlike the familiar courtyard houses of some other Greek cities. She suggests women may have moved less restrictively through these homes. It remains an interpretation of architecture; other Cretan towns had different layouts, and walls cannot tell us every household rule.

sections.title: Written Greek, fresh water and a famous maze

items.text: Between 220 and 209 BCE, a garrison commander at Itanos named Lucius, son of Gaius, dedicated a reservoir and nymphaeum to King Ptolemy IV and Queen Arsinoe III. The inscription identifies him as Roman. People serving an Egyptian dynasty could come from well beyond Egypt or Crete.

Its Greek words “τὸ ὕδρευμα καὶ τὸ νυμφαῖον” mean “the reservoir and the nymphaeum”. The latter was a water feature associated with nymphs. This sample follows the scholarly edition’s accents and spacing. A short carved dedication preserves both a practical water project and the royal names attached to it.

A Knossian coin dated 300 to 200 BCE carries a labyrinth design. The Ashmolean Museum points out that its pattern has a single route to the centre, unlike a puzzle with many wrong turns. The city put its legendary maze onto something small enough to hold in your hand.

ending.text: The map stops at 200 BCE, but Cretan cities continued through further alliances and wars. Roman conquest began in 69 BCE, more than a century later, and Gortyn became the provincial capital. Political independence changed; the island’s communities and urban life continued under Roman rule.
